prompt: In `src/main.tsx`, who calls the function `App` after the first render?
hint: You call React once, on the last lines of the file.

choices.text: Your own code, each time the data changes
choices.why: You never call `App` yourself; that is the framework-like half of React.

choices.text: React, whenever something `App` depends on changes
choices.why: Right. You hand React the component and it decides when to call it.

choices.text: The browser, when the page finishes loading
choices.why: The browser runs `main.tsx`; it knows nothing about components.

choices.text: Vite, once per saved file
choices.why: Vite replaces the module when you save; calling the component is still React's job.

prompt: A colleague says React is "a smaller Angular". What does the section say is the real difference?
hint: The section says it is not size.

choices.text: React has fewer features, so it is quicker to learn
choices.why: Fewer parts is true, and it is the picture the section replaces.

choices.text: Who decides routing, data, forms and the build
choices.why: Right. Angular decides them in one box; React leaves each one to you.

choices.text: Angular is written in TypeScript and React is not
choices.why: This course writes React in TypeScript from lesson 2; the language is not the difference.

choices.text: React runs in the browser and Angular runs on the server
choices.why: Both run in the browser, and both can render on a server too.

prompt: Which description fits React for drawing the screen, and for everything else?
hint: Ask who calls whom in each case.

choices.text: A library for drawing the screen, a framework for everything else
choices.why: The other way round: for everything else React decides nothing.

choices.text: A framework for the screen, a library for the rest
choices.why: Right. React calls your components, and never calls a router it does not know about.

choices.text: A framework in both, since it calls your code
choices.why: It calls components only. Routing and data are calls you make.

choices.text: A library in both, since you install it with npm
choices.why: Angular is installed with npm too; how a package arrives says nothing about who calls whom.

prompt: Match each job to the package this course uses for it.
hint: The table in the section, and the figure before it.

prompt: Why does this course not start with Create React App?
hint: The section calls it a road that is closed.

choices.text: It cannot create projects that use TypeScript, only JavaScript
choices.why: It had a TypeScript template; that is not why it was left behind.

choices.text: It needs a paid account before it will create a project
choices.why: It was free and open source; nothing about it needed an account.

choices.text: Vite is required by React 19
choices.why: React works with any build tool; Vite is this course's choice, not React's requirement.

choices.text: The React team deprecated it in February 2025
choices.why: Right. A course teaching it would teach a tool nobody maintains.

prompt: Why does every lesson install its packages at an exact version?
hint: Think of somebody reading the course a year after it was recorded.

choices.text: Because npm refuses to install a version given as a range
choices.why: npm installs ranges every day; the template's `package.json` is full of them.

choices.text: To make the downloads smaller
choices.why: An exact version is the same size as a version picked from a range.

choices.text: So your code is the transcripts' code
choices.why: Right. A new major version can change an interface and break an example for reasons that are not yours.

choices.text: Because newer versions are less safe to run
choices.why: Newer versions carry fixes; pinning is about reproducing, not about distrust.

prompt: `command -v node` answers `/usr/bin/node`. What does that tell you?
hint: The section says where the course's Node lives.

choices.text: A second Node is answering, not the one in `~/.local`
choices.why: Right. Two Nodes is the situation the setup tries to avoid, and the failures section deals with it.

choices.text: Node is installed correctly, in the folder in your home directory
choices.why: The course's Node answers from `/home/…/.local/bin`; this one does not.

choices.text: npm is missing
choices.why: `command -v` was asked about `node` only; npm is a separate question.

choices.text: The terminal needs to be reopened
choices.why: A terminal that had not read the new `PATH` would answer nothing, not a different folder.

prompt: You are on the virtual-machine path, and your own browser cannot open the app the machine serves. What does the section say is missing?
hint: Two things, and one of them is a flag.

choices.text: A browser installed inside the virtual machine
choices.why: A server has no desktop; the section reads the app from your own computer's browser instead.

choices.text: `--host` on the dev server, and a forwarded port
choices.why: Right. Without `--host` the server answers only inside the machine.

choices.text: A second copy of Node, installed on your own computer as well
choices.why: Node runs in the machine; your computer only needs a browser and a route to the port.

choices.text: A GitHub Codespaces account
choices.why: That is the online path, a different one from the virtual machine.

prompt: What does `^19.3.1` in a `package.json` allow npm to install?
hint: The caret is a range, explained in `javascript` lesson 21.

choices.text: Any 19 from 19.3.1 up
choices.why: Right. Next month that may be 19.4, which is why the course pins.

choices.text: Exactly 19.3.1 and nothing else
choices.why: That is what the version without the caret means.

choices.text: Any version from 19.3.1 up, including 20
choices.why: The caret stops before the next major version.

choices.text: Any 19.3 from 19.3.1 up, but no 19.4
choices.why: That is the tilde, `~19.3.1`, which the template used for TypeScript.

prompt: Why did the course replace the template's `@types/node` 24 with 22.20.5?
hint: Which Node does this course run?

choices.text: Version 24 does not exist yet
choices.why: It exists; the template installed it.

choices.text: It describes Node's interfaces, and this course runs Node 22
choices.why: Right. Nothing broke today, and the right descriptions are still the ones for the Node you run.

choices.text: Version 24 is larger to download and slows down every install
choices.why: Size had nothing to do with it.

choices.text: React 19.3.1 refuses to run with it
choices.why: React never sees `@types/node`; it only describes the build configuration to TypeScript.

prompt: Anybody who clones the project installs exactly what the lockfile says with `npm ___`.
hint: Two letters, and it refuses to start if the two files disagree.

prompt: On which port did the development server answer the first time it ran?
hint: It is in the address it printed.

prompt: `curl` shows the page from the development server carrying a script, `/@react-refresh`, that `index.html` does not have. What would you expect in the build you publish?
hint: What is the script for, and does a visitor need it?

choices.text: The same script, so the published page updates when you save
choices.why: A visitor never saves your files; the script only serves the person editing them.

choices.text: Neither one: a visitor edits nothing
choices.why: Right. The section says neither exists in the build, and lesson 20 compares the two.

choices.text: Only `/@vite/client`, which loads the app
choices.why: That one listens for changed files, which a published page has none of.

choices.text: An error, because `index.html` and the page differ
choices.why: The difference is the development server's doing, and it is expected.

prompt: What does `look` print after the console messages?
hint: One line per thing a screen reader would announce.

choices.text: A screenshot of the page, saved as a PNG file beside it
choices.why: It prints text; a transcript cannot hold an image.

choices.text: The page's HTML source, as the server sent it
choices.why: Only with `--html`, and only the element you name.

choices.text: An accessibility snapshot: roles and names
choices.why: Right. It is the outline a screen reader gives, and what lesson 22's queries use.

choices.text: Every request the page made
choices.why: Only with `--network`.

prompt: The template's hero image is not in the snapshot, while the two logos are. Why?
hint: Look at its `alt`.

choices.text: It failed to load, so there was nothing for the snapshot to show
choices.why: It loaded; a failed image would still be announced by its name.

choices.text: Its empty `alt` marks it as decoration, so it is skipped
choices.why: Right. `alt=""` tells a screen reader there is nothing to announce.

choices.text: `look` skips any image larger than the browser's window
choices.why: `look` has no such rule; the snapshot is the browser's.

choices.text: Only SVG images reach the snapshot
choices.why: The format does not matter; the `alt` does.

prompt: `look` clicked the counter button twice. What number was in its name in the snapshot?
hint: Each `look` starts from a fresh page.

prompt: Why does `look --do` find a button by its role and name, rather than by its position on the page?
hint: The same rule appears in lesson 22.

choices.text: Positions move with the layout; names are what users meet
choices.why: Right. A person, and a screen reader, find a button by what it says.

choices.text: Playwright has no way to read where an element sits on the page
choices.why: It can; this is a choice, and the reason is stability.

choices.text: Buttons have no position until they are clicked
choices.why: Every element on screen has a box from the moment it is drawn.

choices.text: It is quicker for the browser
choices.why: Speed is not the argument the section makes.

prompt: How many minutes does the planner's data plan in the week of Monday 19 October 2026?
hint: One of the six sessions is the week before.

prompt: You rename the course "Organic chemistry" to "Chemistry II" in `courses.json`. What happens to its sessions?
hint: What does a session use to name its course?

choices.text: They stay with it, because they point at its `id`
choices.why: Right. Nothing pointed at the words, so changing the words moves nothing.

choices.text: They detach from it, because they named the old title
choices.why: That is what joining by a name would do, and why the data does not.

choices.text: They move to whichever course is listed just before it
choices.why: Nothing is joined by position either.

choices.text: The JSON stops being valid
choices.why: A different string in a `name` is still valid JSON.

prompt: Why do the transcripts open the planner with `look --today 2026-10-21`?
hint: A transcript is recorded on one day and read on another.

choices.text: So every reading shows the same week
choices.why: Right. The page is told it is Wednesday 21 October 2026, a day in the data's week.

choices.text: Because the app crashes on any other date
choices.why: On another date it shows another week, which is correct and different.

choices.text: Because Playwright has no clock of its own
choices.why: It uses the computer's clock unless told otherwise; that is what `--today` changes.

choices.text: To mark the sessions before that day as done
choices.why: Whether a session is done is in the data, not in the date.

prompt: A second `npm run dev` prints `Port 5173 is in use, trying another one...` and then an address on 5174. What happened?
hint: The section says it is not an error.

choices.text: The second server failed to start and printed why
choices.why: It started, at the next port.

choices.text: The first server was stopped and replaced by this one
choices.why: The first is still running at 5173; nothing stopped it.

choices.text: Vite moved the first server to 5174
choices.why: A running server keeps its port; the new one took the next.

choices.text: Two servers run, and your page is the first one's
choices.why: Right. Stop the one you do not want with Ctrl+C in its terminal.

prompt: Match each message to what it means.
hint: Each one names its own cause, once you know where to look.

pairs.right: The terminal is not in the project's folder
Nothing is listening at that address
An import names a package that is not installed

prompt: Put the steps of this lesson's setup in the order they ran.
hint: The project has to exist before anything is pinned inside it.
items: Install each package at its exact version
`npm run dev`, left running in its own terminal

prompt: Which of these belong in the project's git repository? Choose every one that does.
hint: One of them is 119 MB and is rebuilt from the others.

choices.text: `package.json`
choices.why: Yes: it names what the project needs.

choices.text: `package-lock.json`
choices.why: Yes: it records every package at the version installed, and `npm ci` reads it.

choices.text: `.npmrc`
choices.why: Yes: `save-exact` travels with the project so the next install pins too.

choices.text: `node_modules/`
choices.why: No: the template's `.gitignore` leaves it out, and `npm ci` rebuilds it from the lockfile.
